name: JavaScript
description: Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript for execution. JavaScript (JS) is a platform-independent scripting language (compiled just-in-time at runtime) commonly associated with scripts in webpages, though JS can be executed in runtime environments outside the browser.(Citation: NodeJS) JScript is the Microsoft implementation of the same scripting standard. JScript is interpreted via the Windows Script engine and thus integrated with many components of Windows such as the [Component Object Model](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1559/001) and Internet Explorer HTML Application (HTA) pages.(Citation: JScrip May 2018)(Citation: Microsoft JScript 2007)(Citation: Microsoft Windows Scripts) JavaScript for Automation (JXA) is a macOS scripting language based on JavaScript, included as part of Apple’s Open Scripting Architecture (OSA), that was introduced in OSX 10.10. Apple’s OSA provides scripting capabilities to control applications, interface with the operating system, and bridge access into the rest of Apple’s internal APIs. As of OSX 10.10, OSA only supports two languages, JXA and [AppleScript](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/002). Scripts can be executed via the command line utility osascript, they can be compiled into applications or script files via osacompile, and they can be compiled and executed in memory of other programs by leveraging the OSAKit Framework.(Citation: Apple About Mac Scripting 2016)(Citation: SpecterOps JXA 2020)(Citation: SentinelOne macOS Red Team)(Citation: Red Canary Silver Sparrow Feb2021)(Citation: MDSec macOS JXA and VSCode) Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript to execute various behaviors. Common uses include hosting malicious scripts on websites as part of a [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) or downloading and executing these script files as secondary payloads. Since these payloads are text-based, it is also very common for adversaries to obfuscate their content as part of [Obfuscated Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027).

telemetry.name: Command Execution
telemetry.description: Execution of a command and its interpreter or parent context.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect process command lines and relevant shell/interpreter audit; shell history alone is neither complete nor tamper-resistant.

providers.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
providers.scope: Script content via event 4104 when configured; channel depends on PowerShell edition.

providers.name: Sysmon process events
providers.scope: Interpreter launch and parent context, not full script content.

providers.name: Linux Audit
providers.scope: execve-family execution context; shell built-ins need additional instrumentation.

configuration: Enable Script Block Logging through the policy/configuration for the installed edition. Forward Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational for Windows PowerShell, or PowerShellCore/Operational for PowerShell 7.
Retain script-block ID and fragment ordering alongside process creation. Protect access to collected script text; secrets may be included.
On Linux, use narrowly scoped Audit execution rules for the lab account and supported architectures, and retain joined SYSCALL/EXECVE/PATH records.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Script content and process command lines are different signals. Logging may be partial, fragmented, filtered or disabled; never assume a command line reveals everything executed.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per host role and principal: rare interpreters, command argument patterns and parent-child sequences. Normalize scripts carefully; obfuscation, administrative automation and missing command lines change visibility.

telemetry.name: Module Load
telemetry.description: A module or library being loaded into a running process.
telemetry.collection_focus: Scope Sysmon ImageLoad (7) to lab processes/paths; retain module hash, signer and destination process. Inventory alone does not prove a module loaded.

providers.name: Linux Audit
providers.scope: Linux alternative for supported system-call and file events; different semantics and fields.

providers.scope: macOS alternative where the subscribed event exists; requires an entitled, approved client, not an iOS collector.

configuration: On a disposable Windows host, review the installed Sysmon schema and current configuration; merge scoped event filters into the existing policy rather than replacing it.
Forward Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational to the lab collector. Preserve event ID, timestamp, computer, process identifiers and the original event.
For Linux or macOS, select the equivalent sensor separately and test its emitted fields; a Windows event ID does not transfer across platforms.

atlas_basic.title: T1059.007 JavaScript
atlas_basic.logic: MATCH(script_host_execution) AND script_path IN temporary_or_user_writable_paths -> ALERT

strategies.name: Cross-Platform Detection of JavaScript Execution Abuse

analytics.name: Analytic 0733
analytics.guidance: Detects JavaScript execution through WSH (wscript.exe, cscript.exe) or HTA (mshta.exe), particularly when spawned from Office macros, web browsers, or abnormal user paths. Correlates script execution with outbound network activity or system modification.

tuning.description: Execution of wscript.exe, cscript.exe, or mshta.exe from suspicious parent like Excel or Outlook.
Script loaded from %TEMP%, user download folder, or via UNC/web path.
Execution of JavaScript during non-business or patch windows.
Execution by accounts not typically authorized for scripting (e.g., non-admin users).
Obfuscated JS with high entropy detected by AMSI or ScriptBlock logging.

analytics.name: Analytic 0734
analytics.guidance: Detects JavaScript for Automation (JXA) via osascript or compiled scripts using OSAKit APIs. Flags execution involving system modification, inter-process scripting, or browser abuse.

tuning.description: Execution of JXA from user-controlled paths like ~/Downloads or /Volumes.
osascript invoked by third-party apps (VSCode, browsers, etc.).
Use of OSAKit API by apps not typically scripting-enabled.

analytics.name: Analytic 0735
analytics.guidance: Detects Node.js or JavaScript interpreter execution from web shells, cron jobs, or local users. Correlates execution with reverse shell behavior, file modifications, or abnormal outbound connections.

tuning.description: Script launched from /tmp, /var/tmp, or hidden dot directories.
Custom compiled JS binaries like node_shell or interpreter disguises.
Execution by service accounts or low-privilege users running cron scripts.
Connection attempts to C2 post-node.js execution.

candidates.name: JScript execution to gather local computer information via cscript
candidates.description: JScript execution test, execute JScript via cscript command. When successful, system information will be written to $env:TEMP\T1059.007.out.txt

dependencies.description: Sample script must exist on disk at specified location (#{jscript})

candidates.name: Turla KopiLuwak RC4 Decryption Stager
candidates.description:
Emulates KopiLuwak's next-stage JavaScript loader named Chkdsk.js. The script accepts an
RC4 decryption key via the -scan parameter and decrypts hardcoded ciphertext bytes, which are then run as script.
In this atomic, the decrypted bytes generate and display a random number instead of performing malicious behavior.
In the real attack chain, a scheduled task (ProactiveScan) invokes this script with the key every 30 minutes.

Reference: https://securelist.com/turla-renews-its-arsenal-with-topinambour/91687/

chkdsk_path.description: Path to the KopiLuwak Chkdsk.js stager script

candidates.name: JScript execution to gather local computer information via wscript
candidates.description: JScript execution test, execute JScript via wscript command. When successful, system information will be shown with four message boxes.

dependencies.description: Sample script must exist on disk at specified location (#{jscript})

candidates.name: Turla KopiLuwak Registry JavaScript Payload Execution
candidates.description:
Emulates KopiLuwak's technique of storing a JavaScript payload as REG_BINARY data in the Windows registry
and executing it. The script uses WMI StdRegProv to read binary data from
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Maintenance\MOfficeMaintenance, converts the
bytes to a string with String.fromCharCode, and runs it with eval(). The registry path, value
name, and WMI access pattern mirror the real malware.

Reference: https://securelist.com/turla-renews-its-arsenal-with-topinambour/91687/

payload.description: JavaScript code to store in the registry as binary and execute via eval

registry_script.description: Path to the registry payload JScript file

dependencies.description: Registry payload JScript must exist on disk
Backup existing Maintenance registry key if present
Payload must be written to registry as REG_BINARY

candidates.name: Turla Kopiluwak Windows Enumeration
candidates.description:
Executes a JScript file via wscript.exe that runs a series of reconnaissance commands (net use, ipconfig,
systeminfo, whoami, tasklist, netstat, arp, dir, etc.) and appends all output to a single staging file
at c:\windows\temp\result2.dat. Output file name, wscript.exe execution, and reconnaisance commands run mirror the behaviors of Turla's Javascript trojan Kopiluwak

Reference: https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/turla-pensive-ursa-threat-assessment/

jscript.description: Path to the reconnaissance JScript file

dependencies.description: Reconnaissance JScript must exist on disk
